lines: An erasure request runs through the lakehouse in just minutes, and the ticket closes right away.
An audit days later finds that exact same customer's name sitting in a Kafka topic, in last week's backup, in a marketing export, and in a data scientist's training set.
The lakehouse delete itself was correct, and it was complete.
So which parts of the design were actually missing here, and which of them have no technical answer at all?
answer: The delete operation itself wasn't buggy — it was correct and complete for the lakehouse, and the places the name survived were simply never reached by that operation in the first place.
The real gap sits in every place a table operation never reaches, plus one question that only a lawyer can actually answer.

lines: A subject's own identifier gets traced through classification tags and a lineage graph first.
Then a subject index maps that identifier straight to the exact files and partitions holding them, so a deletion never has to scan the whole lake at all.
That same subject's data can still sit in a spreadsheet, in a model trained on it, or in an export — each one entirely outside the lineage graph's own reach.
A register names every one of those with a human owner attached, rather than pretending the lineage graph already covers it.
A correct delete in one place isn't an erasure process on its own — the blind spots lineage genuinely can't see still need a named owner standing behind them.
Think of the delete as writing forward, not erasing backward.
A fresh snapshot gets written, but the lake's own time-travel feature keeps the previous version reachable until somebody actually expires it.
Setting that expiry clock is the whole design decision, measured against how long the law says it can wait and how long an auditor needs the trail kept.
Delete just one per-subject key, and every copy of that subject's data, including every single backup, becomes unreadable all at once.
That's traded directly against the cost of keeping one key per subject, plus a decryption lookup on every single read.
Crypto shredding trades one per-subject key and a decryption lookup for every copy, including every backup, going unreadable at the exact same instant.
Delete-and-expire's own cost rises both with how often requests arrive and with how long backups get kept around.
Crypto shredding's cost, meanwhile, stays flat once its own up-front key cost is paid.
Those two lines cross at a request rate you can actually compute.
An automated pipeline assembles the snapshot list after expiry, the physical-file listing, the key store's own deletion record, and a repeat search for the subject.
All of that gets emitted for every single request — never produced only once an auditor happens to ask for it.
Proof of deletion is itself a deliverable this pipeline emits on its own, not some auditor's job to go dig up afterward.

Notice what actually turned this from one correct operation into a real process: naming every place the data could hide, picking a schedule or a key strategy by the arithmetic rather than by habit, and never calling it done until the pipeline hands back its own proof.
A second erasure request now arrives for a subject whose data was replicated into a second region before that first request ever landed.
Does the exact same process still find everything it needs to?
answer: Treating it exactly like a single-region request would miss a replica the erasure pipeline never even knew existed.

That's precisely the kind of blind spot this design registers rather than assumes away, so checking the subject index and the blind-spot register for every region the data was placed in follows directly from the register's own purpose.
